extracted.intended_audience: aspiring New Yorker Caption Contest entrants / humor caption writers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and submitting short humorous captions optimized to win the New Yorker Caption Contest, emphasizing image-specificity, voice, brevity, and editorial taste. Includes tactical submission and selection strategies drawn from past winners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be unmistakably anchored to the cartoon image
rubrics_metrics.description: A winning caption must be unmistakably anchored to the cartoon image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The caption should REQUIRE the image to make sense — it should not be a generic one-liner that fits many cartoons. Anti-patterns include captions that are context-free jokes or could apply to any situation; prefer lines that reference something visible or implied in the drawing so the picture and caption form a single comic unit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the SECOND most obvious interpretation (not first or third)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose the second-best interpretation of the scene rather than the first (most obvious) or third (too obscure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first interpretation is what most submitters will write and therefore is overrepresented; the third interpretation is often too obscure for editors and readers. The second-best is slightly unexpected but still clearly readable — the 'sweet spot.' Aim for clarity with a small element of surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the smallest number of words
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the smallest number of words; most winning captions are concise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical winning captions are 4–12 words; cap at under 12. Each unnecessary word is a deduction. Edit out filler phrases like 'I think we should...' down to 'We should...'. Tighten phrasing to increase punch and reduce reading friction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Land on the funniest word at the end
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the funniest word or punchline at the end of the caption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structural payoff matters: positioning the punch word last maximizes comedic impact. Avoid burying the joke in the middle or ending on a weak word. Consider sentence rhythm and the placement of contrast or twist for maximal effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be tonally consistent with the New Yorker's voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Write in a voice consistent with the New Yorker's tone: mildly weary, observational, slightly literate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid TV-sitcom cadence or overly broad sitcom jokes; avoid extreme literary flourishes that feel out of place. Read past finalists to internalize the magazine's mildly ironic, gently sophisticated voice. Tone mismatch is a common reason captions are cut.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't pun unless the pun is essential
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid puns unless the pun is integral to the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Puns are tempting but often feel cheap or overused. Only use a pun if it is essential to the humor and tightly tied to the image; otherwise prefer a cleaner, image-anchored twist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the obvious caption everyone submits
rubrics_metrics.description: Steer clear of the most obvious caption lines that many other submitters will use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study commonly submitted angles and deliberately avoid them. Read historic finalists to absorb editorial taste and notice which obvious angles are repeatedly rejected. Mental exercise: imagine the least funny person you know writing a caption — don't write theirs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission frequency and volume matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Submit regularly — volume and repetition improve odds and help you learn editorial taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Winners recommend submitting weekly. Regular submissions expose you to finalists, letting you internalize the editors' preferences and refine your instincts. Treat submission as iterative practice rather than a one-off.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for cartoon type when choosing strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Different cartoon types have different competitive dynamics and odds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Animals doing human things are the most-submitted and hardest to win; two-figure office cartoons are medium difficulty; surreal scenes (alien landscapes, anthropomorphized objects) are rarer and can offer higher odds to clever captions. Tailor approach: for over-submitted types, aim for a truly fresh angle; for surreal images, bolder cleverness can pay off.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caption Contest Working Rubric (compact checklist)
rubrics_metrics.description: A concise six-point working checklist winners use to evaluate submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The checklist items: (1) Does the caption REQUIRE the image to make sense? (2) Did you choose the 'second-best' interpretation? (3) Is the word count under 12? (4) Is the funniest word last? (5) Is the voice mildly weary, observational? (6) Have you submitted weekly to absorb editor taste? Use this as a quick pre-submit filter to catch common defects.
